present.explain: An Italian verb's ending says who does it: bevo (I drink), bevi (you drink), beve (he or she drinks); vengo, vieni, viene; voglio, vuoi, vuole, vogliamo. Many common verbs change more than their ending, so learn each one's forms as you meet them.
present.why: Italian changes more verb forms for the person than English does: [[bevo]] already says I drink without io.

contrasts.says: Because the ending says who, io and tu can be left out: Bevo caffè.
English drink becomes drinks with he, she or it. Italian distinguishes more people through its verb forms.

mistakes.why: With io, it's bevo.
With tu, it's bevi.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

no-subject.explain: Since the verb's ending says who, Italian usually leaves out io, tu, lui and the rest: Bevo caffè (I drink coffee), Sei pronto? (are you ready?), Mangiamo qui (we're eating here). Say the subject when it matters who, or to contrast two people: Tu sei pronto e io no.
no-subject.why: English needs I or you in front; Italian's ending already says it: [[Bevo]] is I drink, [[Sei]] is you are.

examples.text: Tu sei pronto e io no.
examples.literal: You are ready and I not.

contrasts.says: The ending does the work: bevo, bevi, beve.
English says I in I drink coffee; Italian can leave io out because bevo already identifies the speaker.

mistakes.why: With io the ending is -o; and io can be left out.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

gender.explain: Italian nouns have a grammatical gender: masculine, as in il telefono and il tavolo, or feminine, as in la borsa and la chiave. The masculine singular article can be il or lo, depending on the following sound. Before a vowel, lo and la become l': l'acqua. Articles and adjectives agree with the noun: un caffè, molto caffè but molta acqua, il mio telefono but la mia chiave. Many feminine nouns end in -a and masculine nouns in -o, but not all (la chiave, il latte), so learn the article with each noun.
gender.why: The noun decides, and the words around it follow: [[il]] telefono, [[la]] borsa.

examples.means: The phone is on the table.
examples.literal: The phone is on the table.

examples.means: The bag is on the table.
examples.literal: The bag is on the table.

examples.means: I drink a lot of water.

contrasts.says: English has one the; Italian changes its article for gender, number and the following sound.
mio and mia follow the noun the same way: il mio telefono, la mia chiave.

mistakes.why: telefono is an il word.
borsa is a la word.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

question.explain: A yes-or-no question can keep a statement's order, with intonation marking the question: Sei pronto?, La macchina è qui? A question word or phrase normally comes first: Dov'è la macchina? (dove and è run together), Cosa vuoi fare? Italian does not add a helper like English do.
question.why: English often changes the order or adds do; Italian can ask through intonation: [[Sei pronto]]? is you are ready?

examples.means: What do you want to do?

contrasts.says: English often puts is or a helper like do first. Italian can keep the statement order and use intonation.

mistakes.why: One car: è, run together with dove.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

possessive.explain: Italian normally puts an article before mio and tuo: il mio telefono, la mia chiave, il tuo libro, la tua borsa. mio goes with a masculine singular noun and mia with a feminine singular noun. With unmodified singular family words such as madre and padre, standard Italian normally leaves the article out with mio and tuo: mia madre, tuo padre. Regional or expressive uses of an article with family words also exist.
possessive.why: Italian says the my phone: [[il mio]] telefono, [[la mia]] chiave. The form of my agrees with the possessed noun, not the owner.

examples.text: Il mio telefono è nella borsa.
examples.means: My phone is in the bag.
examples.literal: The my phone is in the bag.

contrasts.says: il mio with il words, la mia with la words.
English says my phone; Italian says the my phone.

mistakes.why: telefono is masculine: mio, not mia.
madre is feminine: mia, not mio.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

articulated.explain: su (on), in (in) and di (of) run into the after them: su + il is sul, in + la is nella, di + la is della. So: sul tavolo (on the table), nella borsa (in the bag), la chiave della macchina (the key of the car). They're never written apart.
articulated.why: Italian joins the little words: [[sul]] tavolo is su il tavolo, on the table, said and written as one word.

examples.means: The phone is on the table.
examples.literal: The phone is on the table.

examples.means: The key is in the bag.
examples.literal: The key is in the bag.

examples.text: La chiave della macchina è qui.
examples.literal: The key of the car is here.

contrasts.says: sul goes with il words; nella and della with la words.
English writes on the as two words; Italian makes them one.

mistakes.wrong: Il telefono è su il tavolo.
mistakes.why: su and il always run together: sul.

mistakes.wrong: La chiave è in la borsa.
mistakes.why: in and la: nella.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons, open to correction.

negation.explain: non goes before the finite verb and any short object pronouns before it: Non bevo caffè, Lei non viene, Non posso leggere. In these modal constructions, it comes before the modal. English often adds do or does; Italian does not need that helper.
negation.why: To negate the whole statement, put [[non]] before the verb: [[Non]] bevo caffè, not I drink coffee.

examples.literal: Not I can read the book.

contrasts.says: English says don't or isn't; Italian says non before the verb.

mistakes.why: With io, use bevo. non stays before the verb.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

modal.explain: After volere (want), potere (can) and dovere (have to), the next verb stays in the infinitive: Voglio mangiare, Puoi leggere questo?, Devo lavorare. The modal changes for the person. No preposition links it to the infinitive, though words such as ancora can come between: Devo ancora lavorare.
modal.why: [[Voglio]] already says I want, so the next verb stays plain: [[Voglio mangiare]], I want eat.

examples.means: I want to drink a coffee.

contrasts.says: The first verb takes the form for who (voglio, vuoi, vuole); the second never does.
English want to has to, whereas can has no to. Italian volere, potere and dovere all take an infinitive without a linking preposition.

mistakes.why: After voglio, the basic form.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

demonstrative.explain: questo goes with an il word and questa with a la word, for this: questo libro, questa chiave. On its own it points at a thing: Questo è un libro, Questa è la mia casa. For that, further away, Italian says quello, which comes later.
demonstrative.why: questo matches the noun like il and la: [[questo]] libro, [[questa]] chiave.

contrasts.says: questo with il words, questa with la words.

mistakes.why: libro is an il word: questo.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons, open to correction.

lei-formal.explain: Lei, written with a capital L in these lessons, is the polite you, used when the relationship or situation calls for formality. It takes a third-person singular verb: Lei vuole un caffè?, Lei sa dov'è?, Lei va a casa? tu is the familiar singular you; voi is plural you.
lei-formal.why: [[Lei]] means you in these examples, not she. It takes the same verb form as lui and lei: [[Lei vuole]], you want.

examples.text: Lei sa dov'è la mia macchina?
examples.means: Do you know where my car is?
examples.literal: You know where is the my car?

contrasts.says: Lei takes the lui and lei form: Lei vuole, Lei sa, Lei va.
English has one you; Italian says tu or Lei by who you're talking to.

mistakes.why: With Lei, the lui and lei form.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

c-e.explain: c'è introduces one person, one thing or something you do not count: C'è qualcuno alla porta. ci sono introduces more than one: Ci sono mio padre e mia madre. When people are expected, ci sono can say they are here or present.
c-e.why: English says there is or there are. Italian puts [[ci]] with essere: [[c'è]] for one, [[ci sono]] for more than one.

examples.literal: There is someone at the door.

examples.text: Ci sono mio padre e mia madre.
examples.means: My father and mother are here.
examples.literal: There are my father and my mother.

contrasts.says: The there in there is introduces something; it does not necessarily mean over there.
è goes with one; sono goes with more than one in ci sono.

mistakes.wrong: Ci sono mio padre e mio madre.
mistakes.right: Ci sono mio padre e mia madre.
mistakes.why: mia agrees with madre, a feminine word.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

adjective-after.explain: A describing word often comes after its noun: una porta aperta, an open door. It agrees with the noun: aperto with libro, aperta with porta. Some adjectives can also come before the noun, sometimes with a different emphasis or meaning; position alone does not make a sentence wrong.
adjective-after.why: English normally puts open before door. Italian can put [[aperta]] after [[porta]] while keeping the same meaning.

examples.means: Is there anyone at the open door?
examples.literal: There is anyone at the door open?

contrasts.says: The ending follows the noun: porta aperta, libro aperto.
English says an open door; Italian says una porta aperta.

mistakes.why: porta is feminine: aperta.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

progressive.explain: stare plus a gerund describes an action in progress. sto cercando means I am looking. The gerund cercando stays the same; sto says who is doing it. The simple present cerco can also describe looking now when the context is clear.
progressive.why: English often uses I am looking for an action happening now. Italian can make that ongoing action explicit with [[sto cercando]].

examples.text: Oggi sto cercando la mia chiave.
examples.means: Today I'm looking for my key.
examples.literal: Today I am looking for the my key.
I am looking in the bag.

contrasts.says: Cerco la chiave can also mean I am looking for the key.
Sto cercando is happening now; Ho perso describes a loss that has happened.

mistakes.why: With io the form of stare is sto, not sta.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

perfect.explain: Ho perso uses avere plus the past participle perso to report a completed loss. ho says I; hai says you. Here perso stays the same for a male or female speaker. Depending on context, ho perso can mean I lost or I have lost.
perfect.why: The past event uses two pieces: [[ho]] and [[perso]]. Learning perdere with perso helps you recognize this irregular past form.

examples.literal: I have lost the your key.

examples.text: Hai perso la chiave anche tu?
examples.means: Have you lost the key too?
examples.literal: You have lost the key also you?

contrasts.says: Cerco la chiave describes the search; Ho perso la chiave describes the earlier loss.
Italian uses this form both where English says I lost and where it says I have lost.

mistakes.why: The helper must agree with io: ho.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

verb-preposition.explain: Learn a verb together with its link to the next word. cercare takes the person or thing directly: Cerco la chiave. English needs for in look for; Italian does not add per. A place can still follow with its own preposition: Cerco la chiave in macchina.
verb-preposition.why: The English phrase look for corresponds to one Italian verb, [[cercare]]. The key is its direct object.

examples.means: I'm looking for the key in the car.
examples.literal: I look for the key in car.

examples.means: I have to look for the phone.
examples.literal: I must look for the phone.

contrasts.says: After devo, use cercare in its basic form.
Do not copy the for from look for into Italian; the verb already connects to the thing sought.

mistakes.why: After devo, use the infinitive cercare. The object follows without a preposition.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

time-telling.explain: alle due means at two o'clock. Use it to say when an appointment or another event happens. alle is a and le written together. There is no separate word for o'clock in these sentences.
time-telling.why: English says at two. Italian says [[alle due]], literally at the two, with the article inside alle.

examples.means: I have an appointment at two o'clock.
examples.literal: I have an appointment at the two.

examples.text: Il mio appuntamento è alle due.
examples.means: My appointment is at two o'clock.
examples.literal: The my appointment is at the two.

contrasts.says: a and le join as alle, just as a and la join as alla.
Do not add a word for o'clock after due here.

mistakes.wrong: Ho un appuntamento a le due.
mistakes.why: a and le must be joined as alle in this time expression.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

conditional.explain: vorrei means I would like. It is the conditional of volere for io, and it makes a wish or request softer than voglio, I want. You can put the requested thing straight after it: Vorrei un appuntamento.
conditional.why: Italian puts the would like meaning into one verb, [[vorrei]]. It is different from voglio, rather than a more polite translation of the same form.

examples.text: Vorrei un appuntamento con il medico.
examples.means: I'd like an appointment with the doctor.
examples.literal: I would like an appointment with the doctor.
I would like an appointment today.

contrasts.says: volere is already familiar in voglio; vorrei is a different form of that verb.
I would like and I want express the same desired thing with different force.

mistakes.why: appuntamento is masculine: un, with no apostrophe before its vowel.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

plural.explain: More than one appuntamento becomes appuntamenti: due appuntamenti. Many masculine nouns ending in -o have a plural in -i, but learn the plural with each noun. Some words, such as caffè, keep the same written form.
plural.why: The number two requires more than one: [[due appuntamenti]]. English adds -s here; Italian changes the ending.

contrasts.says: Gender and number both matter when words agree.
appuntamento changes to appuntamenti; caffè stays caffè even after due.

mistakes.why: With due, use the plural appuntamenti.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

infinitive-links.explain: per followed by an infinitive can explain a purpose: soldi per pagare, money to pay. Here per links the money to what it will be used for. Other expressions have other links; do not put per or another preposition before every infinitive.
infinitive-links.why: English uses to in money to pay. Italian uses [[per pagare]] for this purpose, with pagare in its basic form.

examples.text: Lui non ha soldi per pagare.
examples.means: He doesn't have any money to pay.
examples.literal: He not has money for pay.

contrasts.says: In Posso pagare, potere takes the infinitive without per.
English to can correspond to different Italian links, or to no word at all.

mistakes.why: After per expressing this purpose, use the infinitive pagare, not pago.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

piacere.explain: ci piace says that something is pleasing to us: we like it. The thing or activity being liked determines the verb. A single thing, or an infinitive describing an activity, takes piace: Ci piace questo caffè; Ci piace mangiare insieme.
piacere.why: Italian starts from what is pleasing. [[Ci]] means to us here, and [[piace]] matches the coffee or the activity, not us.

examples.literal: To us is pleasing this coffee.

examples.text: Ci piace mangiare insieme a casa.
examples.means: We like eating together at home.
examples.literal: To us is pleasing eating together at home.

contrasts.says: The English subject is we; in Italian the liked thing or activity is the subject.
ci in ci piace means to us. It has a different job in ci sono, there are.

mistakes.why: One coffee takes piace, even when several people like it.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

avere.explain: avere bisogno di means to need. Keep bisogno unchanged while avere changes with the person: Ho bisogno di aiuto, Hai bisogno di aiuto?, Abbiamo bisogno di aiuto. di connects bisogno to the thing needed.
avere.why: Italian says have need of where English uses need as a verb: [[ho bisogno di]] aiuto.

examples.literal: We have need of a phone.

examples.text: Mio padre ha bisogno di aiuto.
examples.literal: My father has need of help.

contrasts.says: The form of avere says who needs something: ho, hai, ha, abbiamo.
English need corresponds to the whole expression avere bisogno di.

mistakes.why: With io, use ho. bisogno does not change.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

imperative.explain: chiama is a command to one person you say tu to: Chiama il medico, per favore. For chiamare, the tu command ends in -a. A command asks the listener to act; it normally leaves out tu. per favore adds please.
imperative.why: [[Chiama]] asks someone to call. It has the same written form as the statement form for lui or lei, so the situation tells you which job it is doing.

examples.means: Give your father a quick call.

contrasts.says: chiamo describes what I do; chiama can ask you to act.
Like English Call the doctor, an Italian command usually leaves out the listener as subject.

mistakes.why: With singular medico, use singular il, not plural i.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

object-pronoun.explain: mi means me and ti means you when they are short objects. They go right before a verb like aspetto or aspetti: Ti aspetto, I wait for you; Mi aspetti?, will you wait for me? The verb ending still says who is waiting. non goes before the pronoun and verb. With an affirmative command to tu, the pronoun joins the end instead (aspettami); that comes later.
object-pronoun.why: In [[Ti aspetto]], ti is the person being waited for; aspetto says I am doing the waiting. English puts you after wait for.

examples.means: Will you wait for me here?
I'm not waiting for you here.
examples.literal: Not you I wait for here.

contrasts.says: The subject can be left out: aspetto already says I. ti is the object, not the subject.
Italian puts ti before aspetto; English puts you after wait for.

mistakes.why: With io, use aspetto. ti still means you, the person waited for.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

di.explain: di connects a container to what is in it: una tazza di caffè, a cup of coffee. It can also connect a thing to its owner: la tazza di mia madre, my mother's cup. Here mia madre has no article; di stays separate.
di.why: English uses of for the contents and often 's for an owner. Italian uses [[di]] in both these phrases.

examples.means: I'll have a cup of coffee.
examples.literal: I take a cup of coffee.

examples.text: La tazza di mia madre è qui.
examples.literal: The cup of my mother is here.

contrasts.says: la tazza di mia madre names the owner; la mia tazza uses my.
When di meets a definite article, it joins it, as in della macchina.

mistakes.wrong: La tazza di mio madre è qui.
mistakes.right: La tazza di mia madre è qui.
mistakes.why: mia agrees with madre, a feminine word.

source.note: Written with the Italian lessons 21–40, open to correction.
